messages.author: bcfb6bc9f75aae0f
messages.subject: Re: [BUGS] A few places remain: Bayesian Biostatistics: Special Topics(BBST); University of Edinburgh,Scotland, UK
parts:
Well, BUGS (more precisely Jags, nowadays..) still has its points :
  • discrete parameters sampling ;
  • (much) less type/declaration nitpicking* : a vector is the same thing as a row vector wich is the same thing as a real[], a matrix is a matrix, etc...  (OTOH, no way to declare restrictions or constraints...) ;
  • DAG are a "natural" form of expressing a lot of problems (in my case, medical statistics) ;
  • "natural" automatic handling of missing data (again, a strong point with those pesky medical datasets...) ;
  • Some (questionable) use of the DAG structure (e. g. automated DIC computation).
I still think that a "SuperBUGS" language, subsuming BUGS and able to use more efficient sampling methods, would have a lot of use cases...

Currently, Stan is a great language for applied mathematicians working on Bayesian statistical problems. But a lot of statistics users are biologists, physicians, engineers, etc..., looking for a valid way to think about biological, medical, engineering, etc... problems in terms of probabilities. To them, the larger technical overhead of Stan can be perceived as a hurdle.

Another possible hurdle is the availability of resources : on an "normal" Linux installation, the minimal memory needed to compile even the simplest Stan program is about 4,5 Gb (thanks to Boost, I think). This means that you can't use it on an average laptop without swapping somehow. In Windows, this means trashing (and in Linux, to a somewhat lesser extend...), and Stan gets a bad rap...

None of this reasons is sufficient, or even serious. But their conjunction steers a lot of end-users away from Stan towards Jags.

HTH,

--
Emmanuel Charpentier

* I'm starting to consider C++ as the non-conventional infectious agent (a bit like a prion) of a neurological disease, which, among other symptoms, is the alteration of the perception of practicality. Consider the discussion on the "new form of sampling statements" discussion(s) in stan-devel and tell me with a straight face that's not pathological...

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: [BUGS] A few places remain: Bayesian Biostatistics: Special Topics(BBST); University of Edinburgh,Scotland, UK
parts:
> On Feb 29, 2016, at 5:49 AM, Emmanuel Charpentier <emanuel.c...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Well, BUGS (more precisely Jags, nowadays..) still has its points :
> • discrete parameters sampling ;

This is almost always a bad idea computationally, but
I agree that users like to be able to write it. The models
I have that I used to struggle with in BUGS/JAGS fit in
a snap in Stan when I marginalize out the discrete parameters (two
examples you can use for comparison are in the marginalizing
discrete parameters chapter of the manual).

> • (much) less type/declaration nitpicking* : a vector is the same thing as a row vector wich is the same thing as a real[], a matrix is a matrix, etc... (OTOH, no way to declare restrictions or constraints...) ;

What's best for simple models isn't necessarily what's
best for more complex models. We really geared Stan toward
being able to write more complex models.

Also, we wanted to be able to write down linear algebra
statements naturally and do type inference at compile time
to catch potential bugs.

> • DAG are a "natural" form of expressing a lot of problems (in my case, medical statistics) ;

Agreed, but they're also limiting in more complex cases.

> • "natural" automatic handling of missing data (again, a strong point with those pesky medical datasets...) ;

It still requires modeling and a simple univariate prior on
the missing data is rarely what you want.

> • Some (questionable) use of the DAG structure (e. g. automated DIC computation).
> I still think that a "SuperBUGS" language, subsuming BUGS and able to use more efficient sampling methods, would have a lot of use cases...
That's what NIMBLE is trying to do. And PyMC to some extent.

> Currently, Stan is a great language for applied mathematicians working on Bayesian statistical problems. But a lot of statistics users are biologists, physicians, engineers, etc..., looking for a valid way to think about biological, medical, engineering, etc... problems in terms of probabilities. To them, the larger technical overhead of Stan can be perceived as a hurdle.

They've told us as much themselves. Others building complex models
have found it liberating. It's really very hard to please everyone (and
I didn't mean that sarcastically).

> Another possible hurdle is the availability of resources : on an "normal" Linux installation, the minimal memory needed to compile even the simplest Stan program is about 4,5 Gb (thanks to Boost, I think). This means that you can't use it on an average laptop without swapping somehow. In Windows, this means trashing (and in Linux, to a somewhat lesser extend...), and Stan gets a bad rap...
We could seriously use a better C++ compiler technology!
> None of this reasons is sufficient, or even serious. But their conjunction steers a lot of end-users away from Stan towards Jags.
Agreed.

>
> HTH,
>
> --
> Emmanuel Charpentier
>
> * I'm starting to consider C++ as the non-conventional infectious agent (a bit like a prion) of a neurological disease, which, among other symptoms, is the alteration of the perception of practicality. Consider the discussion on the "new form of sampling statements" discussion(s) in stan-devel and tell me with a straight face that's not pathological...

C++ is a classic example of something that's very complex and
very useful for hard problems (like autodiff and efficient matrix
libraries and custom memory management) but overkill for a lot of
simple problems where C or Java (or even Python or R) would be just
fine.

There aren't any statements that do sampling in Stan, so we
want to try to clear up misconceptions users have to that end
(which they also have about BUGS/JAGS). The goal's not at
all related to C++. It's related to the fact that a Stan program
defines a log density rather than being required to lay out a generative
model a la BUGS (for better or worse).

- Bob
